title: AI'm Not Doing the Homework
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Jo Castelino, author of The Homework Conundrum, argues that generative AI has intensified a problem homework has always faced - students taking shortcuts to avoid the effort that produces real learning - to the point where teachers must fundamentally rethink homework's design and purpose. She distinguishes information (instantly accessible facts) from knowledge (which must be built through effortful engagement), noting that without robust foundational knowledge students cannot fully comprehend new concepts even with instant access to information. Drawing on David Didau's argument that AI amplifies thinking only when students think first and use it afterward, Castelino describes how some students now scan homework questions into apps that generate full step-by-step solutions, converting homework into pure copying with zero cognitive engagement. She builds on Craig Barton's proposed fix - pairing AI-vulnerable homework with an AI-free in-class quiz on the same content - while cautioning that a poor quiz score doesn't always mean a student skipped their homework, since memory performance genuinely fluctuates. Her own concrete proposals are threefold: ask the same or similar question in the next lesson as a quick effort-check, have students narrate their thinking aloud on homework-linked content (which AI cannot fake), and deliberately build a whole-school culture - reinforced by how teachers, heads of year, and headteachers talk about homework - where its connection to classroom learning is made explicit and visible.
points: Castelino's key conceptual distinction: students today have 'information at their fingertips,' not knowledge - and without robust foundational knowledge already built, they cannot fully comprehend new concepts even with instant information access.

Her illustrative example of the problem's scale: students showed her an app that scans a maths homework question and generates a full step-by-step solution for them to copy, 'with no thinking involved.'

Building on Craig Barton's proposed fix (an AI-free in-class quiz on recent homework content), Castelino adds an important caveat: a poor quiz score doesn't always mean a student skipped their homework - memory performance can genuinely fluctuate day to day.

Her first concrete strategy - 'similar questions' - asks the same or a closely related question from the homework during the next lesson (e.g., via mini-whiteboards) as a quick, low-stakes signal of engagement.

Her second strategy - 'narrate their thinking' - has students articulate their reasoning aloud on homework-linked content in class, a check AI-generated answers cannot fake, reinforced by a school-wide culture where homework's link to classroom learning is made explicit.
quotes: Our students are so used to finding things out quickly. Some people say this is a good thing because they've got knowledge at their fingertips. This is incorrect. They have information at their fingertips.
So, without robust foundational knowledge, students will find it difficult to fully comprehend a concept.
They scan the question and the app generates a full step-by-step response to the question. The student then simply copies the answer and they've completed their homework with no thinking involved!

Students have always looked for ways to take shortcuts or avoid the hard work when it comes to homework... Now AI makes it even simpler to bypass the effort, but the challenge of encouraging genuine learning remains the same.
But we cannot assume a poor quiz score in lessons equates a lack of effort with homework.
We must protect the integrity of independent learning and help students engage meaningfully with their work.
